September 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 3
Presidential RamblingsBy Steve Fairbairn
The GVWG 2021/22 season begins this month and
we will be kicking off the new season with a
presentation by North Carolina artist/sculptor
Roberto Ferrer who will be demonstrating “Wall
Sculptures Made Easy”. This should prove to be
an extremely interesting presentation.
Our new season also means that it is time to renew your GVWG membership. For the first time,
you are now able to renew your membership
online and pay your dues via etransfer, if that is
more convenient for you. Of course, we will still
be accepting cheques via snail mail. Full details
on how to renew online can be found on our website.
I hope you all enjoyed the virtual video and slide
show tours of several of our members’ workshops/studios
during
our
August
monthly
meeting. From the small to the grand dream
shops toured, each displayed features and ideas
that we can all adopt in our own spaces. If you
missed them, or would like to review them again,
we posted the video recording on the net. You
will have received an email with the link to the
video. As with all videos that the GVWG shares
exclusively with its members, please do not share
the links with others.
As we get closer to 2022, we are looking forward
to hopefully being back in Sapperton Pensioners
Hall for our monthly meetings early in the new
year. As you can imagine, the dates and required
safety precautions are bit fluid at the moment but
we will keep everyone updated as we learn more.
When we return to physical meetings our hope is
to be able to conduct “hybrid” meetings where
we stream our physical meetings in real time so
remote members or those who are not able or
wanting to travel to the meetings are able to view
and interact with the meeting. Our club tech gurus are busy working out the technical challenges
involved with this and we hope to have a working
solution in time for our first in-person meetings.
In anticipation of meeting in person once again, I
would like to renew the call for one or more volunteers for the Educational Coordinator role that
has been available for several months. The Educational Coordinator(s) are responsible for recruiting and scheduling the monthly meeting
presentations. I can’t stress how critical this role
is for the success of the guild and how important
it is to have one or more people in place as soon
as possible. If you are interested in stepping up
for this role, or would like more information as to
what is involved, please contact me or any other
GVWG board member.
Another volunteer role that has come up is Membership Coordinator. This role is responsible for
accepting new member applications and payments at our physical meetings and, with the assistance of our Treasurer, maintain the official
membership list. This is not an onerous role and
would be great for anyone who would like to get
more involved with the guild.
The Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guild is
completely volunteer operated. As woodturning
clubs go, the GVWG is one of the more successful
organizations and that is due, in no small part, to
the efforts of the many volunteers over the years
who have stepped up and done their part to make
this club what it is today. As our club ages, so do
our members and volunteers. To maintain the
level and quality of offerings the club brings to its
members, we must continue to bring new volunteers onboard. Taking on a volunteer role is rewarding and is a great way to get more involved
with the guild as well as meet and become more
familiar with other members. If you are interested in becoming more involved, please contact me
or any other board member.

Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 5
This bowl is made from Catalpa and is embellished
with a technique using Kroma Crackle. This can be
obtained from Kroma on Granville Island or from
Opus. It is a fairly clear liquid that crackles as it
dries. It can be mixed with acrylic colours to a
maximum of 5% so I am using a digital scale when
mixing the products.
The bowl was first finished with a water-based lacquer then the base colour of white acrylic was applied.
Now comes the fun part, trying to put on the Kroma Crackle. Kroma Crackle is fairly thin and tends
to run off of 3 dimensional objects. I taped up the
surfaces I didn't want covered and put it on the
lathe driven by a block of styrofoam on the inside
of the bowl and a ball providing tension on the tailstock. I applied the product and then turned the
lathe on at a very slow speed. Don't forget to put
waste sheets under the bowl to catch the slop. This
keeps the product on the surface however until the
crackle starts setting you still need to manipulate
its distribution.
I had a heat lamp directed towards the surface to
enhance drying. In discussions with Kroma, you
could also let the product sit and thicken before
applying it. The reason this one has such a variation in thin areas vs thick areas is the heat light
burnt out on me midway. What an opportunity!!
There is another issue that arose that I am working
on a solution for. When you have your lathe turning slowly the motor tends to overheat so you may
need to have a fan directed at the motor. AC motors rely on them turning at a fairly good speed to
drive the mechanical cooling fan.
After the surface is dry you can remove the tape
and clean up any areas that have media where you
don't want it and then you need to apply several
additional coats of finish to protect the crackle.
The crackle may curl when it dries and when I
sprayed the additional coats it tended to flatten
out the curl, or you could force it to flatten into the
new finish with a toothpick.
I have done many test boards with this product and
am looking for more ways to use this product.
Golden makes a product called Crackle paste and it
doesn't run like this product however it doesn't
seem to develop as appealing a crackle texture as
the background doesn't show through as much.
I got this idea from watching a video by Joanne
Sauvageau so you may want to check her
out. There are also many videos on this product on
YouTube.
You can manipulate this with a heat gun and also
do dry brushing techniques on it or come up with
your own ideas. Have fun and don't stop playing.

Still StandingBy Sheila Balzer, WIT Liaison
Wow, another month has gone by. We’re slowly
getting back into the flow of routines, the GVWG is
launching its membership renewal, and some are
looking forward to transitioning from the garden
and outside activities to the shop and indoor activities again. During this fall season I’m looking forward to connecting with both old and new members, and my list of projects to work on is growing.
Much has happened
since
I
became
a
woodturner in August
2020. While I have always had a love and
appreciation for trees,
during my most recent
wandering
through
Beacon Hill Park in Victoria I was seeing the
trees in a new light and
with even more curiosity. So many interesting
shapes, forms, textures, and species. Multiple
states of growth and decay.
It is also the season that
I’m hearing more chainsaws and chippers.
I now realize that I have
begun
balancing
the
desire of saving each
tree, as I’d prefer to see
them standing, with salvaging and saving those
that come down so they
can
continue
to be
something else.
Does anyone else have a visceral response to the
sound of grinding timber? Ok, perhaps for some of
the branches, but anything over 3” in diameter can
be so much more? And the bigger chunks make a
horrific sound being ground. Hanging onto it for
fuel seems better than
grinding,
although
grinding seems to be
the way of the world
given the desire to
transform
large
amounts of material
into
manageable
heaps. Saving the best
bits from the grinder is
satisfying,
but
it
doesn’t take long before the shop/space is
filled with more chunks of wood than anyone can
possibly turn in a lifetime.
As wood turners, we’re ultimately making chips
too. We’re just slower at it and having way more
fun making them.

Guild Member Profile
- Claudia Hayward
By Claudia Hayward
I’ve always been interested in working with wood.
My dad was a basement hobbyist who encouraged
my participation - he was very broadminded for a
time when girls were more into sewing and cooking. Much to my mother’s disappointment, neither
of those things interested me.
When I was in university, my dad and I built an 8 ft
sailboat – I remember using the drill press to rout a
channel down the mainmast.
After graduating from university I taught school for
a couple of years and was then accepted as one of
two token women (this was the 70’s remember) in
the Fish and Wildlife Program at BCIT . At the same
time I met the guy who was to become my husband. When we moved in together we had almost
no furniture but the local school board offered
woodworking courses in night school. I took one
and built a coffee table. Then we decided to build
a canoe, which we stored on the deck of our apartment. We ultimately bought a house with a nice
big basement which soon became a workshop.
After running out of people to give our projects to,
it was time to look into other options and we became involved with selling at craft fairs. In those
days any handmade crafty items sold like crazy and
we found it sufficiently lucrative that my husband
quit his teaching job and I left my job as a technician with an environmental company. We did major craft shows from Vancouver to Winnipeg, selling gift items – cheeseboards, trivets, cutting
boards and other flatwork. For a time we also did
pottery which worked very well when combined
with the wood.
This went on for 25 years until my husband became too ill to work. After he passed away I was
looking for a new direction, I didn’t know what I
wanted but I went to the Wood Show at Cloverdale
and discovered the GVWG demonstrating wood
turning. And so it began.
The Shop
(Continued on page 8)

September 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 8
Early on our big basement workshop became very
small and we needed a dedicated space. We found
property in Maple Ridge, the first thing to go up
was the shop, the house took a little longer. It’s a
great area, approximately 600 sq ft with a loft for
storage. Even then it would be nice to have more
space! Lots of good woodworking tools, planer,
jointer, belt sander, thickness sander, drill press,
tablesaw, and my Oneway 1640. I’m on 5 acres so
I have a lot of space outside for cutting up wood.
My Approach to Woodturning
I’m not an artist. I don’t have many, if any, creative
bones in my body. I like doing functional work and
within reason, I like doing production. I admire
those of you who come up with wonderful jigs, artistic and creative pieces, but my mind just doesn’t
work that way. I suspect it comes from the many
years of doing woodwork that had to sell in order
to pay bills. I like to sell my work so I can make
more and I appreciate the numerous compliments
that I receive at craft shows, the ultimate compliment being that someone will give you money for
something you have made. Not many jobs give
one such positive reinforcement on a regular basis.
I enjoy the interaction with customers and other
crafters and I’ve made many lifelong friends over
the years.
My Work
Early on we realized that success in the craft show
business is variety in what you make. For several
years we became potters as well as woodworkers,
making mugs, bowls and a variety of other ceramics. Combined with the woodworking it gave us a
new look. Although I no longer do pottery, I still
make a few ceramic tiles which I inset into boards
for unique trivets and cheeseboards.
These days I am always on the search for functional
items that I can make in my shop. I like to take the
basic idea and see how I can improve the look and
function to make something I can produce. It usually takes a lot of trial and error (usually 10 or
more attempts- if it’s going to work!) to come up
an item that I will be able to sell.
My favourite turning project is bowls. Each one is a
challenge to get the right curve and each piece of
wood works differently. I also like turning rolling
pins, the challenge there is to get straight lines.
I’ve played around a bit with dyes, and hope to do
more. Between turning and flat work, I always
have something different to work on.
Materials and Finishing
For many years we worked primarily in teak. Back
in the day teak was all the rage and it was reasona-
(Continued from page 7)
(Continued on page 9)

September 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 9
bly priced. It was the perfect wood for most of the
items we made. Strong, easy to work (carbide
tipped blades on all machines were a must), easy
to finish - it is an incredibly durable wood. Won’t
stain or mark from heat – perfect for kitchenware.
As tastes changed and Scandinavian furniture became less fashionable, we continued to use teak
but began to incorporate black walnut. Today I
work primarily in maple, although I still use a limited amount of teak (plantation grown in Costa Rica) for one of my items. Maple is an obvious
choice since much of my work is bowls. I also use
black walnut and maple for my flat work.
Finishing is as time consuming as the making of the
item. I use General Wood Bowl Finish on any item
that will come in contact with food. I find it is easy
to apply, durable and as the old saying goes, shiny
sells. I’ve also tried Osmo Polyx and like it. Wipe
on Poly is also great and I use it on items such as
handles and peppermills. Even mineral oil has limited use although it never really dries.
Display/Selling
I’m fortunate enough to have been in the business
long enough to have established a presence and a
(good, I hope) reputation. I’ve been a member of
Circle Craft for more than 30 years and have done
their craft shows since the beginning at Vancouver
East Cultural Centre. I still sell some of my work
through their shop on Granville Island. I no longer
do major craft sales across the country but do the
Christmas sale at the Vancouver Convention Centre
and Out of Hand in Victoria.
I do a few sales through the summer through Vancouver Farmer’s Market at Trout Lake. I also have
work at the Maple Ridge Art Gallery. I enjoy my
work but I’ve got lots of other things to do – I play
tennis, hike, like to garden and there’s always a lot
to do with a 5 acre property . I’m also finding that
sourcing wood is becoming very time consuming –
and getting more difficult to get good wood. And
then there’s the prep time before even getting it
on the lathe.
Where Am I Going?
I’m happy doing what I’m doing. There are always
challenges even with work that one has done many
(Continued from page 8)
(Continued on page 10)

September 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 10
times before. I like the physicality of prepping
wood, I enjoy making shavings and I like going to
shows, meeting people and selling my work. At this
time in my life it has become a hobby more than a
job. I love what I do and I consider myself so fortunate to have been able to make a living doing
woodwork.
(Continued from page 9)

Safety
-Fires & Extinguishers
By Allan Cusworth reporting on a presentation by Ed Pretty
Editor’s Note: This is an excerpt from our June 2008
newsletter article by Allan Cusworth.
Classes of Fires
Class A - Normal combustibles: Wood, paper, etc.
Use cooling and quenching to extinguish - an ABC
type extinguisher is OK.
Class B - Flammable Liquids: This is a misnomer as
liquids, and solids for that matter, do not burn –
vapours do. Heat vaporizes the materials to create
the vapour that burns. Do not use water to extinguish - it spreads the fire around. Use a dry powder extinguisher to remove the source of oxygen -
an ABC extinguisher is OK. CO2 will work but is not
recommended since it dissipates and the fire can
restart.
Class C - Energized Electrical: The key word here is
“energized”. You must shut off the power source
first. The fire then becomes A or B Class and can be
dealt with as above.
Class D - Flammable Metals: Metals such as Sodium, Magnesium, and Lithium will ignite and burn
and are almost impossible to extinguish. Do not
use water as it will cause a major explosion and
spread the fire rapidly. The fire must be encapsulated and allowed to burn itself out. Use carbon to
encase the fire ball.
(Continued on page 12)
Ed brought thirty six years of experience in the fire
service to our meeting and it certainly showed. His
presentation was not only informative, but also
dramatic and even humorous.
How to Choose, Maintain, and Place an ABC Fire Extinguisher
The best type of ABC class fire extinguisher has a metal head. It should also have a hose and nozzle to
direct the powder discharge at the base of the fire easier.
DO NOT TEST it! If you do, the pressure will bleed down and the extinguisher will be useless.
Over time, the powder will settle and become hard. It should slosh when you shake the extinguisher. To
check it, use a RUBBER mallet to tap the bottom and sides to release the powder till it sloshes. Also,
check the pressure gauge.
A fire extinguisher should be located near the exits of the room. You should always be able to keep yourself between the fire and the door so you will not get trapped by the fire.

September 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 12
Shop Fire?
The best class of fire extinguisher to have in your
shop is an ABC since most of the materials are either normal combustibles, or flammable liquids. A
water hose is good only for small fires.
Call the Fire Department!

In Memoriam
- Al Timms
By Tom Wilson, Fraser Valley Woodturners Guild President
It is with much regret that I inform you that our recent FVWG President Al
Timms passed away Friday morning peacefully at Abbotsford Regional Hospital. At this time of sorrow the family is asking you for privacy. The family has
also asked that flowers not to be sent and that if one wishes, donations can
be made to the Heart Foundation of BC.
Al worked and lived and was well respected in this community. His time and
efforts that he shared with our Guild will be remembered fondly.
Al will greatly be missed.
At a future date there will be a Celebration of Life.

Safety Guidelines for WoodturningYou mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility
 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 28)

September 2021
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 28
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.

while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
